candidates.statement: The purpose of this guidance is to describe the benefit-risk assessment framework that the 17 Agency uses in evaluating whether applications for opioid analgesic drugs meet the standard for 18 approval under section 505 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. This guidance 19 summarizes the information that should be included in a new drug application for an opioid 20 analgesic drug to facilitate the Agency’s benefit-risk assessment. 21

candidates.context: The following sections describe the information that FDA will consider in assessing the benefits 65 and risks of an opioid analgesic drug. Consistent with the benefit-risk assessment framework, 66 FDA considers the benefits and risks to the patient when the drug is used as labeled, as well as 67 the benefits and risks relative to other available therapies for pain. Additionally, FDA considers 68 the public health risks of the drug related to misuse, abuse, opioid use disorder, accidental 69 exposure, and overdose in both patients and nonpatients, as well as any properties of the drug 70 that may mitigate such risks. Note that the risk of opioid use disorder can arise even when a 71 patient is taking an opioid analgesic drug as labeled. 72 A. Benefits to the Patient Using the Drug as Labeled 77

candidates.statement: − To support the opioid-specific public health benefit-risk evaluation, the applicant 187 should use traditional epidemiologic data sources (e.g., surveys, emergency 188 department visits, poison control center calls) and nontraditional sources (e.g., 189 internet discussion forums and blogs, social media, qualitative/ethnographic studies, 190 law enforcement data) to provide information about how this moiety or similar opioid 191 analgesic drugs are misused and abused in postmarketing settings. These data should 192 address demographic patterns of abuse, the routes by which these drugs are abused, 193 concomitant abuse of other substances, as well as risks of related adverse outcomes 194 (e.g., addiction, fatal and nonfatal overdose, infectious complications of abuse). 195

candidates.statement: 4 See the Opioid Analgesic Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy web page at https://www.fda.gov/Drugs/DrugSafety/InformationbyDrugClass/ucm163647.htm . Note that certain opioid analgesic drugs are subject to other REMS. Information on the specific REMS associated with each approved opioid analgesic drug can be found on the FDA’s Approved Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies (REMS) web page at https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cder/rems/index.cfm .
candidates.context: FDA has determined that a class-wide risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS) is 232 necessary for all opioid analgesic drugs intended for outpatient use to ensure that the benefits of 233 these drugs continue to outweigh the risks. 4 The Opioid Analgesic REMS program requires that 234 training be made available to all health care providers (HCPs) who are involved in the 235 management of patients with pain, including nurses and pharmacists. 5 To meet this requirement, 236 drug companies with approved opioid analgesic drugs provide unrestricted grants to accredited 237 continuing education providers for the development of education courses for HCPs based on 238

candidates.statement: To the extent that the safety profile of a drug product may differ from those drug products 242 covered by the class-wide REMS, a product-specific REMS or REMS element may be required. 243 For example, an opioid analgesic drug that must be restricted to use in a monitored inpatient 244 setting may need additional risk mitigation strategies to ensure the drug product does not leave 245 the hospital. In short, the applicant for an opioid analgesic drug should include any proposed 246 REMS that the applicant considers necessary to ensure a drug’s benefits outweigh its risks. All 247 sponsors of opioid analgesic drugs should begin discussions with FDA early during drug 248 development regarding product-specific risks and the potential need for additional risk 249 mitigation. 250
